{{Short description|Ratio of the perimeter of Bernoulli's lemniscate to its diameter}}
{{Redirect|Gauss's constant|the parameter used in orbital mechanics|Gaussian gravitational constant}}
[[File:Lemniscate of Bernoulli.svg|thumb|Lemniscate of Bernoulli]]
In [[mathematics]], the '''lemniscate constant''' {{mvar|ϖ}} is a [[transcendental number|transcendental]] mathematical constant that is the ratio of the [[perimeter]] of [[Lemniscate of Bernoulli|Bernoulli's lemniscate]] to its [[Diameter of a set|diameter]], analogous to the definition of [[Pi|{{pi}}]] for the circle.<ref>See:
* {{Cite book |last1=Gauss |first1=C. F. |title=Werke (Band III)|publisher=Herausgegeben der Königlichen Gesellschaft der Wissenschaften zu Göttingen |language=Latin, German|year=1866|url=https://gdz.sub.uni-goettingen.de/id/PPN235999628}} p. 404
* {{harvnb|Cox|1984|p=281}}
* {{Cite book |last1=Eymard |first1=Pierre |last2=Lafon| first2=Jean-Pierre |title=The Number Pi |publisher=American Mathematical Society |year=2004 |isbn=0-8218-3246-8}} p. 199
* {{cite book |last1=Bottazzini |first1=Umberto |authorlink1=Umberto Bottazzini |last2=Gray |first2=Jeremy |authorlink2=Jeremy Gray (mathematician) |date=2013 |title=Hidden Harmony – Geometric Fantasies: The Rise of Complex Function Theory |publisher=Springer |doi=10.1007/978-1-4614-5725-1 |isbn=978-1-4614-5724-4 }} p. 57
* {{Cite book |last1=Arakawa |first1=Tsuneo |last2=Ibukiyama| first2=Tomoyoshi |last3=Kaneko|first3=Masanobu|title=Bernoulli Numbers and Zeta Functions |publisher=Springer |year=2014 |isbn=978-4-431-54918-5}} p. 203</ref> Equivalently, the perimeter of the lemniscate <math>(x^2+y^2)^2=x^2-y^2</math> is <math>2\varpi</math>. The lemniscate constant is closely related to the [[lemniscate elliptic functions]] and is approximately equal to 2.62205755.<ref>See:
* {{harvnb|Finch|2003|p=420}}
* {{citation|title=Applications of generalized trigonometric functions with two parameters|last1=Kobayashi|first1=Hiroyuki|last2=Takeuchi|first2=Shingo|journal=Communications on Pure & Applied Analysis|arxiv=1903.07407|year=2019|volume=18|issue=3|pages=1509–1521|doi=10.3934/cpaa.2019072|s2cid=102487670}}
* {{citation|title=Elliptic Gauss Sums and Hecke L-values at s=1|last1=Asai|first1=Tetsuya|arxiv=0707.3711|year=2007}}
* {{cite web | url=http://oeis.org/A062539 | title=A062539 - Oeis }}</ref> It also appears in evaluation of the [[Particular values of the gamma function|gamma]] and [[beta function]] at certain rational values. The symbol {{mvar|ϖ}} is a [[cursive]] variant of {{mvar|π}} known as [[variant pi]] represented in Unicode by the character {{unichar|03D6}}.

Sometimes the quantities {{math|2''ϖ''}} or {{math|''ϖ/2''}} are referred to as ''the'' lemniscate constant.<ref>{{Cite web | url=http://oeis.org/A064853 | title=A064853 - Oeis }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.numberworld.org/digits/Lemniscate/|title=Lemniscate Constant}}</ref>

== History ==

'''Gauss's constant''', denoted by ''G'', is equal to {{math|''ϖ'' / {{pi}} ≈ 0.8346268}}<ref>{{cite web |title=A014549 - Oeis |url=http://oeis.org/A014549}}</ref> and named after [[Carl Friedrich Gauss]], who calculated it via the [[arithmetic–geometric mean]] as <math>1/M\bigl(1,\sqrt{2}\bigr)</math>.{{sfn|Finch|2003|p=420}} By 1799, Gauss had two proofs of the theorem that <math>M\bigl(1,\sqrt2\bigr)=\pi/\varpi</math> where <math>\varpi</math> is the lemniscate constant.<ref>Neither of these proofs was rigorous from the modern point of view. See {{harvnb|Cox|1984|p=281}}</ref>

[[Jack Todd (mathematician)|John Todd]] named two more lemniscate constants, the ''first lemniscate constant'' {{math|1=''A'' = ''ϖ''/2 ≈ 1.3110287771}} and the ''second lemniscate constant'' {{math|1=''B'' = {{pi}}/(2''ϖ'') ≈ 0.5990701173}}.<ref name="todd">{{Cite journal |last=Todd |first=John |date=January 1975 |title=The lemniscate constants |journal=[[Communications of the ACM]] |volume=18 |pages=14–19 |doi=10.1145/360569.360580 |s2cid=85873 |doi-access=free |number=1}}</ref><ref name="lemniscate constant A">{{Cite web |title=A085565 - Oeis |url=http://oeis.org/A085565}} and {{cite web |title=A076390 - Oeis |url=http://oeis.org/A076390}}</ref><ref>{{dlmf|first=B. C.|last=Carlson|id=19.20.E2|title=Elliptic Integrals}}</ref>

The lemniscate constant <math>\varpi</math> and Todd's first lemniscate constant <math>A</math> were proven [[transcendental number|transcendental]] by [[Carl Ludwig Siegel]] in 1932 and later by [[Theodor Schneider]] in 1937 and Todd's second lemniscate constant <math>B</math> and Gauss's constant <math>G</math> were proven transcendental by Theodor Schneider in 1941.{{r|todd}}<ref>In particular, Siegel proved that if <math>\operatorname{G}_4(\omega_1,\omega_2)</math> and <math>\operatorname{G}_6(\omega_1,\omega_2)</math> with <math>\operatorname{Im}(\omega_2/\omega_1)>0</math> are algebraic, then <math>\omega_1</math> or <math>\omega_2</math> is transcendental. Here, <math>\operatorname{G}_4</math> and <math>\operatorname{G}_6</math> are [[Eisenstein series]]. The fact that <math>\varpi</math> is transcendental follows from <math>\operatorname{G}_4(\varpi,\varpi i)=1/15</math> and <math>\operatorname{G}_6(\varpi,\varpi i)=0.</math> {{pb}} {{Cite book |last=Apostol |first=T. M. |title=Modular Functions and Dirichlet Series in Number Theory|publisher=Springer |year=1990 |isbn=0-387-97127-0|page=12|edition=Second}}  {{pb}} {{Cite journal |last=Siegel |first=C. L. |date=1932 |title=Über die Perioden elliptischer Funktionen. |url=https://eudml.org/doc/149791 |journal=[[Crelle's Journal|Journal für die reine und angewandte Mathematik]] |volume=167 |pages=62–69|doi=10.1515/crll.1932.167.62 |language=German}}</ref><ref>In particular, Schneider proved that the [[beta function]] <math>\Beta (a,b)</math> is transcendental for all <math>a,b\in\mathbb{Q}\setminus\mathbb{Z}</math> such that <math>a+b\notin \mathbb{Z}_0^-</math>. The fact that <math>\varpi</math> is transcendental follows from <math>\varpi=\tfrac{1}{2}\Beta \bigl(\tfrac{1}{4},\tfrac{1}{2}\bigr)</math> and similarly for {{mvar|B}} and {{mvar|G}} from <math>\Beta \bigl(\tfrac{1}{2},\tfrac{3}{4}\bigr).</math> {{pb}} {{cite journal |first=Theodor |last=Schneider |url=https://www.deepdyve.com/lp/de-gruyter/zur-theorie-der-abelschen-funktionen-und-integrale-mn0U50bvkB |title=Zur Theorie der Abelschen Funktionen und Integrale |year=1941 |journal=Journal für die reine und angewandte Mathematik |volume=183 |number=19 |pages=110–128 |doi=10.1515/crll.1941.183.110 |s2cid=118624331 }}</ref> In 1975, [[Gregory Chudnovsky]] proved that <math>\pi</math> and <math>\varpi</math> are [[Algebraic independence|algebraically independent]] over <math>\mathbb{Q}</math>, which implies that <math>A</math> and <math>B</math> are algebraically independent as well.<ref>G. V. Choodnovsky: ''Algebraic independence of constants connected with the functions of analysis'', Notices of the AMS 22, 1975, p. A-486</ref><ref>G. V. Chudnovsky: ''Contributions to The Theory of Transcendental Numbers'', American Mathematical Society, 1984, p. 6</ref> But the set <math>\bigl\{\pi,M\bigl(1,1/\sqrt{2}\bigr),M'\bigl(1,1/\sqrt{2}\bigr)\bigr\}</math> (where the prime denotes the [[derivative]] with respect to the second variable) is not algebraically independent over <math>\mathbb{Q}</math>.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Borwein |first1=Jonathan M. |last2=Borwein| first2=Peter B. |title=Pi and the AGM: A Study in Analytic Number Theory and Computational Complexity |publisher=Wiley-Interscience |year=1987 |edition=First |isbn=0-471-83138-7}} p. 45</ref> In fact,
<math display="block">\pi=2\sqrt{2}\frac{M^3\left(1,\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)}{M'\left(1,\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)}=\frac{1}{G^3 M'\left(1,\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)}.</math>
In 1996, [[Yuri Nesterenko (mathematician)|Yuri Nesterenko]] proved that {{math|[[Gelfond's constant|''e''<sup>''π''</sup>]]}}, <math>\pi</math>, and <math>\varpi</math> are algebraically independent over <math>\mathbb{Q}</math>.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Nesterenko |first1=Y. V. |last2=Philippon|first2=P.|title=Introduction to Algebraic Independence Theory|publisher=Springer |year=2001 |isbn=3-540-41496-7|page=27}}</ref>

As of 2025 over 2 trillion digits of this constant have been calculated using [[y-cruncher]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Yee |date=May 18, 2025 |first=Alexander J. |type=Personal website |title=Records set by y-cruncher |url=http://numberworld.org/y-cruncher/records.html |access-date=2025-05-19 |website=Numberworld}}</ref>

== Forms ==

Usually, <math>\varpi</math> is defined by the first equality below, but it has many equivalent forms:<ref>See:
* {{harvnb|Cox|1984|p=281}}
* {{harvnb|Finch|2003|pp=420–422}}
* {{cite book  |chapter=Some milestones of lemniscatomy  |last1=Schappacher |first1=Norbert |author-link1=Norbert Schappacher | date= 1997 |editor1-last=Sertöz |editor1-first=S. |title=Algebraic Geometry |type=Proceedings of Bilkent Summer School, August 7–19, 1995, Ankara, Turkey |publisher=Marcel Dekker |pages=257–290 | chapter-url=http://irma.math.unistra.fr/~schappa/NSch/Publications_files/1997_LemniscProvis.pdf}}</ref>

<math display="block">\begin{aligned}
\varpi
&= 2\int_0^1\frac{dt}{\sqrt{1-t^4}}
 = \sqrt2\int_0^\infty\frac{dt}{\sqrt{1+t^4}}
 = \int_0^1\frac{dt}{\sqrt{t-t^3}}
 = \int_1^\infty \frac{dt}{\sqrt{t^3-t}}\\[6mu]
&= 4\int_0^\infty\Bigl(\sqrt[4]{1+t^{4}}-t\Bigr)dt
 = 2\sqrt2\int_0^1 \sqrt[4]{1-t^{4}}\mathop{dt} =3\int_0^1 \sqrt{1-t^4}dt\\[2mu]
&= 2K(i)
 = \tfrac{1}{2}\Beta\bigl( \tfrac14, \tfrac12\bigr)
 = \tfrac{1}{2\sqrt2}\Beta\bigl( \tfrac14, \tfrac14\bigr)
 = \frac{\Gamma (1/4)^2}{2\sqrt{2\pi}}
 = \frac{2-\sqrt2}{4}\frac{\zeta(3/4)^2}{\zeta(1/4)^2}\\[5mu]
&= 2.62205\;75542\;92119\;81046\;48395\;89891\;11941\ldots,
\end{aligned}</math>

where {{mvar|K}} is the [[Elliptic integral#Complete elliptic integral of the first kind|complete elliptic integral of the first kind]] with modulus {{mvar|k}}, {{math|&Beta;}} is the [[beta function]], {{math|&Gamma;}} is the [[gamma function]] and {{mvar|ζ}} is the [[Riemann zeta function]].

The lemniscate constant can also be computed by the [[arithmetic–geometric mean]] <math>M</math>,

<math display=block>\varpi=\frac{\pi}{M\bigl(1,\sqrt2\bigr)}.</math>

Gauss's constant is typically defined as the [[Multiplicative inverse|reciprocal]] of the [[arithmetic–geometric mean]] of 1 and the [[square root of 2]], after his calculation of <math>M\bigl(1, \sqrt2\bigr)</math> published in 1800:{{sfn|Cox|1984|p=277}}<math display="block">G = \frac{1}{M\bigl(1, \sqrt2\bigr)}</math>John Todd's lemniscate constants may be given in terms of the [[beta function]] B:
<math display="block">\begin{aligned}
A &= \frac\varpi2 = \tfrac14 \Beta \bigl(\tfrac14,\tfrac12\bigr), \\[3mu]
B &= \frac{\pi}{2\varpi} =\tfrac14\Beta \bigl(\tfrac12,\tfrac34\bigr).
\end{aligned}</math>

===As a special value of L-functions===
<math display=block>\beta'(0)=\log\frac{\varpi}{\sqrt{\pi}}</math>

which is analogous to

<math display=block>\zeta'(0)=\log\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}</math>

where <math>\beta</math> is the [[Dirichlet beta function]] and <math>\zeta</math> is the [[Riemann zeta function]].<ref>{{cite web | url=http://oeis.org/A113847 | title=A113847 - Oeis }}</ref>

Analogously to the [[Leibniz formula for π]],
<math display="block">\beta (1)=\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{\chi (n)}{n}=\frac{\pi}{4},</math>
we have<ref>{{cite book |last=Cremona |first=J. E. |date= 1997 |edition=2nd|title=Algorithms for Modular Elliptic Curves|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=MtM8AAAAIAAJ|publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]]|isbn=0521598206}} p. 31, formula (2.8.10)</ref><ref>In fact, the series <math display="inline">\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{\nu (n)}{n^s}</math> converges for <math>\operatorname{\Re}s>5/6</math>.</ref><ref>{{cite book |last=Murty |first=Vijaya Kumar |author-link=V. Kumar Murty|date= 1995 |page=16 |title=Seminar on Fermat's Last Theorem |publisher= [[American Mathematical Society]]|isbn=9780821803134}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book| last=Cohen| first=Henri|author-link=Henri Cohen (number theorist)|date=1993|pages=382–406|title=A Course in Computational Algebraic Number Theory|publisher=Springer-Verlag|isbn=978-3-642-08142-2}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.lmfdb.org/EllipticCurve/Q/32/a/3 |title=Elliptic curve with LMFDB label 32.a3 (Cremona label 32a2)|website=The L-functions and modular forms database}}</ref>
<math display="block">L(E,1)=\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{\nu (n)}{n}=\frac{\varpi}{4}</math>
where <math>L</math> is the [[L-function]] of the [[elliptic curve]] <math>E:\, y^2=x^3-x</math> over <math>\mathbb{Q}</math>; this means that <math>\nu</math> is the [[multiplicative function]] given by
<math display="block">\nu (p^n)=\begin{cases}
p - \mathcal{N}_p,                   & p\in\mathbb{P}, \, n=1 \\[5mu]
0,                                   & p=2,\, n\ge 2 \\[5mu]
\nu (p)\nu (p^{n-1})-p\nu (p^{n-2}), & p\in\mathbb{P}\setminus\{2\},\, n\ge 2
\end{cases}</math>
where <math>\mathcal{N}_p</math> is the number of solutions of the congruence
<math display="block">a^3-a\equiv b^2 \,(\operatorname{mod}p),\quad p\in\mathbb{P}</math>
in variables <math>a,b</math> that are non-negative integers (<math>\mathbb{P}</math> is the set of all primes).
Equivalently, <math>\nu</math> is given by
<math display="block">F(\tau)=\eta (4\tau)^2\eta (8\tau)^2=\sum_{n=1}^\infty \nu (n) q^n,\quad q=e^{2\pi i\tau}</math>
where <math>\tau\in\mathbb{C}</math> such that <math>\operatorname{\Im}\tau >0</math> and <math>\eta</math> is the [[Dedekind eta function|eta function]].<ref>The function <math>F</math> is the unique weight <math>2</math> level <math>32</math> [[Modular form#Types|new form]] and it satisfies the functional equation
:<math>F\left(-\frac{1}{\tau}\right)=-\frac{\tau^2}{32}F\left(\frac{\tau\vphantom1}{32}\right).</math></ref><ref>The <math>\nu</math> function is closely related to the <math>\xi</math> function which is the multiplicative function defined by
:<math>\xi (p^n) = \begin{cases}
\mathcal{N}_p',             & p\in\mathbb{P},\, n=1 \\[5mu]
\xi (p^{n-1}) + \chi (p)^n, & p\in\mathbb{P},\, n\ge 2
\end{cases}</math>
where <math>\mathcal{N}_p'</math> is the number of solutions of the equation
:<math>a^2+b^2=p,\quad p\in\mathbb{P}</math>
in variables <math>a,b</math> that are non-negative integers (see [[Fermat's theorem on sums of two squares]]) and <math>\chi</math> is the [[Dirichlet character]] from the Leibniz formula for π; also
:<math>\sum_{d|n}\chi (d)=\xi (n)</math>
for any positive integer <math>n</math> where the sum extends only over positive divisors; the relation between <math>\nu</math> and <math>\xi</math> is
:<math>\sum_{k=0}^n (-1)^k \xi (4k+1)\xi (4n-4k+1)=\nu (2n+1)</math>
where <math>n</math> is any non-negative integer.</ref><ref>The <math>\nu</math> function also appears in
:<math>\sum_{z\in\mathbb{G};\, z\overline{z}=n}z=\nu (n)</math>
where <math>n</math> is any positive integer and <math>\operatorname{\mathbb{G}}</math> is the set of all [[Gaussian integer]]s of the form
:<math>(-1)^{\frac{a\pm b-1}{2}}(a\pm bi)</math>
where <math>a</math> is odd and <math>b</math> is even. The <math>\xi</math> function from the previous note satisfies
:<math>\left|\{z:z\in\mathbb{G}\and z\overline{z}=n\}\right|=\xi (n)</math>
where <math>n</math> is positive odd.</ref>
The above result can be equivalently written as
<math display="block">\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{\nu (n)}{n}e^{-2\pi n/\sqrt{32}}=\frac{\varpi}{8}</math>
(the number <math>32</math> is the [[Conductor of an elliptic curve|conductor]] of <math>E</math>) and also tells us that the [[Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture|BSD conjecture]] is true for the above <math>E</math>.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Rubin |first=Karl |date=1987 |title=Tate-Shafarevich groups and L-functions of elliptic curves with complex multiplication |url=https://eudml.org/doc/143493 |journal=Inventiones Mathematicae |volume=89 |issue=3 |page=528|doi=10.1007/BF01388984 |bibcode=1987InMat..89..527R }}</ref>
The first few values of <math>\nu</math> are given by the following table; if <math>1\le n\le 113</math> such that <math>n</math> doesn't appear in the table, then <math>\nu (n)=0</math>:
<math display="block">\begin{array}{r|r|r|r}
n & \nu (n) & n & \nu (n) \\ 
\hline
1 & 1 & 53 & 14 \\
5 & -2 & 61 & -10 \\
9 & -3 & 65 & -12 \\ 
13 & 6 & 73 & -6 \\
17 & 2 & 81 & 9 \\
25 & -1 & 85 & -4 \\ 
29 & -10 & 89 & 10\\
37 & -2 & 97 & 18 \\
41 & 10 & 101 & -2 \\
45 & 6 & 109 & 6 \\
49 & -7 & 113 & -14 \\
\end{array}</math>

===As a special value of other functions===
Let <math>\Delta</math> be the minimal weight level <math>1</math> new form. Then<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.lmfdb.org/ModularForm/GL2/Q/holomorphic/1/12/a/a/|title=Newform orbit 1.12.a.a|website=The L-functions and modular forms database}}</ref>
<math display="block">\Delta (i)=\frac{1}{64}\left(\frac{\varpi}{\pi}\right)^{12}.</math>
The <math>q</math>-coefficient of <math>\Delta</math> is the [[Ramanujan tau function]].

== Series ==
[[Viète's formula]] for {{mvar|π}} can be written:

<math display=block>
\frac2\pi = \sqrt\frac12 \cdot \sqrt{\frac12 + \frac12\sqrt\frac12} \cdot \sqrt{\frac12 + \frac12\sqrt{\frac12 + \frac12\sqrt\frac12}} \cdots
</math>

An analogous formula for {{mvar|ϖ}} is:<ref>Levin (2006)</ref>

<math display=block>
\frac2\varpi = \sqrt\frac12 \cdot \sqrt{\frac12 +  \frac12 \bigg/ \!\sqrt\frac12} \cdot \sqrt{\frac12 +  \frac12 \Bigg/ \!\sqrt{\frac12 +  \frac12 \bigg/ \!\sqrt\frac12}} \cdots
</math>

The [[Wallis product]] for {{mvar|π}} is:

<math display=block>
\frac{\pi}{2} = \prod_{n=1}^\infty \left(1+\frac{1}{n}\right)^{(-1)^{n+1}}=\prod_{n=1}^{\infty} \left(\frac{2n}{2n-1} \cdot \frac{2n}{2n+1}\right)
= \biggl(\frac{2}{1} \cdot \frac{2}{3}\biggr) \biggl(\frac{4}{3} \cdot \frac{4}{5}\biggr) \biggl(\frac{6}{5} \cdot \frac{6}{7}\biggr) \cdots
</math>

An analogous formula for {{mvar|ϖ}} is:<ref>Hyde (2014) proves the validity of a more general Wallis-like formula for clover curves; here the special case of the lemniscate is slightly transformed, for clarity.</ref>

<math display=block>
\frac{\varpi}{2} = \prod_{n=1}^\infty \left(1+\frac{1}{2n}\right)^{(-1)^{n+1}}=\prod_{n=1}^{\infty} \left(\frac{4n-1}{4n-2} \cdot \frac{4n}{4n+1}\right)
= \biggl(\frac{3}{2} \cdot \frac{4}{5}\biggr) \biggl(\frac{7}{6} \cdot \frac{8}{9}\biggr) \biggl(\frac{11}{10} \cdot \frac{12}{13}\biggr) \cdots
</math>

A related result for Gauss's constant (<math>G=\varpi / \pi</math>) is:<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Hyde |first1=Trevor |year=2014 |title=A Wallis product on clovers |journal=The American Mathematical Monthly |volume=121 |issue=3 |pages=237–243 |url=https://math.uchicago.edu/~tghyde/Hyde%20--%20A%20Wallis%20product%20on%20clovers.pdf |doi=10.4169/amer.math.monthly.121.03.237 |s2cid=34819500 |archive-date=2021-10-16 |access-date=2021-10-29 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211016003137/https://math.uchicago.edu/~tghyde/Hyde%20--%20A%20Wallis%20product%20on%20clovers.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref>

<math display="block">
\frac{\varpi}{\pi} = \prod_{n=1}^{\infty} \left(\frac{4n-1}{4n} \cdot \frac{4n+2}{4n+1}\right)
= \biggl(\frac{3}{4} \cdot \frac{6}{5}\biggr) \biggl(\frac{7}{8} \cdot \frac{10}{9}\biggr) \biggl(\frac{11}{12} \cdot \frac{14}{13}\biggr) \cdots
</math>

An [[infinite series]] discovered by Gauss is:<ref>{{cite book |last1=Bottazzini |first1=Umberto |authorlink1=Umberto Bottazzini |last2=Gray |first2=Jeremy |authorlink2=Jeremy Gray (mathematician) |date=2013 |title=Hidden Harmony – Geometric Fantasies: The Rise of Complex Function Theory |publisher=Springer |doi=10.1007/978-1-4614-5725-1 |isbn=978-1-4614-5724-4 }} p. 60</ref>

<math display="block">
\frac{\varpi}{\pi} = \sum_{n=0}^\infty (-1)^n \prod_{k=1}^n \frac{(2k-1)^2}{(2k)^2}  
= 1 - \frac{1^2}{2^2} + \frac{1^2\cdot3^2}{2^2\cdot4^2} - \frac{1^2\cdot3^2\cdot5^2}{2^2\cdot4^2\cdot6^2} + \cdots
</math>

The [[Machin-like formula|Machin formula]] for {{mvar|π}} is <math display=inline>\tfrac14\pi = 4 \arctan \tfrac15 - \arctan \tfrac1{239},</math> and several similar formulas for {{mvar|π}} can be developed using trigonometric angle sum identities, e.g. Euler's formula <math display=inline>\tfrac14\pi = \arctan\tfrac12 + \arctan\tfrac13</math>. Analogous formulas can be developed for {{mvar|ϖ}}, including the following found by Gauss: <math>\tfrac12\varpi = 2 \operatorname{arcsl} \tfrac12 + \operatorname{arcsl} \tfrac7{23}</math>, where <math>\operatorname{arcsl}</math> is the [[Lemniscate elliptic functions#Inverse functions|lemniscate arcsine]].<ref>Todd (1975)</ref>

The lemniscate constant can be rapidly computed by the series<ref>{{harvnb|Cox|1984|p=307|loc=eq. 2.21}} for the first equality. The second equality can be proved by using the [[pentagonal number theorem]].</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last1=Berndt |first1=Bruce C. |title=Ramanujan's Notebooks Part V |publisher=Springer |year=1998 |isbn=978-1-4612-7221-2}} p. 326</ref>

:<math>\varpi=2^{-1/2}\pi\biggl(\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}e^{-\pi n^2}\biggr)^2=2^{1/4}\pi e^{-\pi/12} \biggl(\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}(-1)^n e^{-\pi p_n}\biggr)^2</math>

where <math>p_n=\tfrac12(3n^2-n)</math> (these are the [[pentagonal number|generalized pentagonal numbers]]). Also<ref>This formula can be proved by [[List of formulae involving π#Hypergeometric inversions|hypergeometric inversion]]: Let
:<math>\operatorname{a}(q)=\sum_{m,n\in\mathbb{Z}}q^{m^2+mn+n^2}</math>
where <math>q\in\mathbb{C}</math> with <math>\left|q\right|<1</math>. Then
:<math>\operatorname{a}(q)={}_2F_1\left(\frac{1}{3},\frac{2}{3},1,z\right)</math>
where
:<math>q=\exp\left(-\frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{3}}\frac{{}_2F_1(1/3,2/3,1,1-z)}{{}_2F_1(1/3,2/3,1,z)}\right)</math>
where <math>z\in\mathbb{C}\setminus\{0,1\}</math>. The formula in question follows from setting <math display="inline">z=\tfrac14\bigl(3\sqrt{3}-5\bigr)</math>.</ref>

:<math>\sum_{m,n\in\mathbb{Z}}e^{-2\pi (m^2 +mn+n^2)}=\sqrt{1+\sqrt{3}}\dfrac{\varpi}{12^{1/8}\pi}.</math>

In a spirit similar to that of the [[Basel problem]],
:<math>\sum_{z\in\mathbb{Z}[i]\setminus\{0\}}\frac{1}{z^4}=G_4(i)=\frac{\varpi ^4}{15}</math>
where <math>\mathbb{Z}[i]</math> are the [[Gaussian integers]] and <math>G_4</math> is the [[Eisenstein series]] of weight {{tmath|4}} (see [[Lemniscate elliptic functions#Hurwitz numbers|Lemniscate elliptic functions § Hurwitz numbers]] for a more general result).<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Eymard |first1=Pierre |last2=Lafon| first2=Jean-Pierre |title=The Number Pi |publisher=American Mathematical Society |year=2004 |isbn=0-8218-3246-8}} p. 232</ref>

A related result is
:<math>\sum_{n=1}^\infty \sigma_3(n)e^{-2\pi n}=\frac{\varpi^4}{80 \pi^4}-\frac{1}{240}</math>
where <math>\sigma_3</math> is the [[Divisor function|sum of positive divisors function]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www-users.math.umn.edu/~garrett/m/mfms/notes_2015-16/10_level_one.pdf |title=Level-one elliptic modular forms |last=Garrett |first=Paul |website=University of Minnesota}} p. 11—13</ref>

In 1842, [[Carl Johan Malmsten|Malmsten]] found
:<math>\beta'(1)=\sum_{n=1}^\infty (-1)^{n+1}\frac{\log (2n+1)}{2n+1}=\frac{\pi}{4}\left(\gamma+2\log\frac{\pi}{\varpi\sqrt{2}}\right)</math>

where <math>\gamma</math> is [[Euler's constant]] and <math>\beta(s)</math> is the Dirichlet-Beta function.

The lemniscate constant is given by the rapidly converging series

<math display="block">\varpi = \pi\sqrt[4]{32}e^{-\frac{\pi}{3}}\biggl(\sum_{n = -\infty}^\infty (-1)^n e^{-2n\pi(3n+1)} \biggr)^2.</math>

The constant is also given by the [[infinite product]]

:<math>\varpi = \pi\prod_{m = 1}^\infty \tanh^2 \left( \frac{\pi m}{2}\right).</math>

Also<ref>The formula follows from the [[Generalized hypergeometric function|hypergeometric]] transformation
:<math>{}_3F_2\left(\frac14,\frac12,\frac34,1,1,16z\frac{(1-z)^2}{(1+z)^4}\right)=(1+z)\,{}_2F_1\left(\frac12,\frac12,1,z\right)^2</math>
where <math>z=\lambda (1+5i)</math> and <math>\lambda</math> is the [[modular lambda function]].</ref>
:<math>\sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{(-1)^n}{6635520^n}\frac{(4n)!}{n!^4}=\frac{24}{5^{7/4}}\frac{\varpi^2}{\pi^2}.</math>

== Continued fractions ==
A (generalized) [[continued fraction]] for {{mvar|π}} is
<math display="block">\frac\pi2=1 + \cfrac{1}{1 + \cfrac{1\cdot 2}{1 + \cfrac{2\cdot 3}{1 + \cfrac{3\cdot 4}{1+\ddots}}}}</math>
An analogous formula for {{mvar|ϖ}} is{{r|lemniscate constant A}}
<math display="block">\frac\varpi2= 1 + \cfrac{1}{2 + \cfrac{2\cdot 3}{2 + \cfrac{4\cdot 5}{2 + \cfrac{6\cdot 7}{2+\ddots}}}}</math>

Define ''[[William Brouncker, 2nd Viscount Brouncker|Brouncker]]'s continued fraction'' by<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Khrushchev |first1=Sergey |title=Orthogonal Polynomials and Continued Fractions |publisher=Cambridge University Press |year=2008 |edition=First |isbn=978-0-521-85419-1}} p. 140 (eq. 3.34), p. 153. There's an error on p. 153: <math>4 [\Gamma(3+s/4)/\Gamma(1+s/4)]^2</math> should be <math>4[\Gamma((3+s)/4)/\Gamma((1+s)/4)]^2</math>.</ref>
<math display="block">b(s)=s + \cfrac{1^2}{2s + \cfrac{3^2}{2s + \cfrac{5^2}{2s+\ddots}}},\quad s>0.</math>
Let <math>n\ge 0</math> except for the first equality where <math>n\ge 1</math>. Then<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Khrushchev |first1=Sergey |title=Orthogonal Polynomials and Continued Fractions |publisher=Cambridge University Press |year=2008 |edition=First |isbn=978-0-521-85419-1}} p. 146, 155</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last1=Perron |first1=Oskar |language=German |author-link=Oskar Perron|title=Die Lehre von den Kettenbrüchen: Band II |publisher=B. G. Teubner |year=1957 |edition=Third}} p. 36, eq. 24</ref>
<math display="block">\begin{align}b(4n)&=(4n+1)\prod_{k=1}^n \frac{(4k-1)^2}{(4k-3)(4k+1)}\frac{\pi}{\varpi^2}\\
b(4n+1)&=(2n+1)\prod_{k=1}^n \frac{(2k)^2}{(2k-1)(2k+1)}\frac{4}{\pi}\\
b(4n+2)&=(4n+1)\prod_{k=1}^n \frac{(4k-3)(4k+1)}{(4k-1)^2}\frac{\varpi^2}{\pi}\\
b(4n+3)&=(2n+1)\prod_{k=1}^n \frac{(2k-1)(2k+1)}{(2k)^2}\,\pi.\end{align}</math>
For example,
<math display="block">\begin{align}
b(1) &= \frac{4}{\pi}, &
b(2) &= \frac{\varpi^2}{\pi}, &
b(3) &= \pi, &
b(4) &= \frac{9\pi}{\varpi^2}.
\end{align}</math>

In fact, the values of <math>b(1)</math> and <math>b(2)</math>, coupled with the functional equation
<math display="block">b(s+2)=\frac{(s+1)^2}{b(s)},</math>
determine the values of <math>b(n)</math> for all <math>n</math>.

===Simple continued fractions===
Simple continued fractions for the lemniscate constant and related constants include<ref>{{Cite web |title=A062540 - OEIS |url=http://oeis.org/A062540 |access-date=2022-09-14 |website=oeis.org}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=A053002 - OEIS|url=http://oeis.org/A053002|website=oeis.org}}</ref>
<math display="block">\begin{align}
\varpi           &= [2,1,1,1,1,1,4,1,2,\ldots], \\[8mu]
2\varpi          &= [5,4,10,2,1,2,3,29,\ldots], \\[5mu]
\frac{\varpi}{2} &= [1,3,4,1,1,1,5,2,\ldots], \\[2mu]
\frac{\varpi}{\pi} &= [0,1,5,21,3,4,14,\ldots].
\end{align}</math>

== Integrals ==

[[File:Lemniscate constant as an integral.png|thumb|upright=1.3|A geometric representation of <math>\varpi/2</math> and <math>\varpi/\sqrt{2}</math>]]
The lemniscate constant {{mvar|ϖ}} is related to the area under the curve <math>x^4 + y^4 = 1</math>. Defining <math>\pi_n \mathrel{:=} \Beta\bigl(\tfrac1n, \tfrac1n \bigr)</math>, twice the area in the positive quadrant under the curve <math>x^n + y^n = 1</math> is <math display=inline>2 \int_0^1 \sqrt[n]{1 - x^n}\mathop{\mathrm{d}x} = \tfrac1n \pi_n.</math> In the quartic case, <math>\tfrac14 \pi_4 = \tfrac1\sqrt{2} \varpi.</math>

In 1842, Malmsten discovered that<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Blagouchine |first1=Iaroslav V. |date=2014 |title=Rediscovery of Malmsten's integrals, their evaluation by contour integration methods and some related results |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/257381156 |journal=The Ramanujan Journal |volume=35 |issue=1 |pages=21–110|doi=10.1007/s11139-013-9528-5 |s2cid=120943474 }}</ref>

<math display=block>\int_0^1 \frac{\log (-\log x)}{1+x^2}\, dx=\frac{\pi}{2}\log\frac{\pi}{\varpi\sqrt{2}}.</math>

Furthermore,
<math display=block>\int_0^\infty \frac{\tanh x}{x}e^{-x}\, dx=\log\frac{\varpi^2}{\pi}</math>

and<ref>{{cite web | url=https://oeis.org/A068467 | title=A068467 - Oeis }}</ref>

<math display="block">\int_0^\infty e^{-x^4}\, dx=\frac{\sqrt{2\varpi\sqrt{2\pi}}}{4},\quad\text{analogous to}\,\int_0^\infty e^{-x^2}\, dx=\frac{\sqrt{\pi}}{2},</math>
a form of [[Gaussian integral]].

The lemniscate constant appears in the evaluation of the integrals

<math display="block"> {\frac{\pi}{\varpi}} = \int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\sqrt{\sin(x)}\,dx=\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\sqrt{\cos(x)}\,dx </math>

<math display="block"> \frac{\varpi}{\pi} = \int_0^{\infty}{\frac{dx}{\sqrt{\cosh(\pi x)}}} </math>

John Todd's lemniscate constants are defined by integrals:{{r|todd}}

<math display=block>A = \int_0^1\frac{dx}{\sqrt{1 - x^4}}</math>

<math display=block>B = \int_0^1\frac{x^2\, dx}{\sqrt{1 - x^4}} </math>

=== Circumference of an ellipse ===

The lemniscate constant satisfies the equation{{sfn|Cox|1984|p=313}}

<math display="block">\frac{\pi}{\varpi} = 2 \int_0^1\frac{x^2\, dx}{\sqrt{1 - x^4}} </math>

Euler discovered in 1738 that for the rectangular elastica (first and second lemniscate constants)<ref>Levien (2008)</ref>{{sfn|Cox|1984|p=313}}

<math display=block>\textrm{arc}\ \textrm{length}\cdot\textrm{height} = A \cdot B = \int_0^1 \frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\sqrt{1 - x^4}} \cdot \int_0^1 \frac{x^2 \mathop{\mathrm{d}x}}{\sqrt{1 - x^4}} = \frac\varpi2 \cdot \frac\pi{2\varpi} = \frac\pi4</math>

Now considering the circumference <math>C</math> of the [[ellipse]] with axes <math>\sqrt{2}</math> and <math>1</math>, satisfying <math>2x^2 + 4y^2 = 1</math>, Stirling noted that{{sfn|Cox|1984|p=312}}

<math display="block"> \frac{C}{2} = \int_0^1\frac{dx}{\sqrt{1 - x^4}} + \int_0^1\frac{x^2\,dx}{\sqrt{1 - x^4}}</math>

Hence the full circumference is

<math display="block"> C = \frac{\pi}{\varpi} + \varpi =3.820197789\ldots </math>

This is also the [[arc length]] of the [[Sine and cosine|sine]] curve on half a period:<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.ams.org/notices/201208/rtx120801094p.pdf|title=An Eloquent Formula for the Perimeter of an Ellipse|last=Adlaj|first=Semjon|date=2012|website=American Mathematical Society|page=1097|quote=One might also observe that the length of the “sine” curve over half a period, that is, the length of the graph of the function {{tmath|1=\sin(t)}} from the point where {{tmath|1=t = 0}} to the point where {{tmath|1=t = \pi}} , is <math>\sqrt{2} l(1/\sqrt{2}) = L + M</math>.}} In this paper <math>M=1/G=\pi/\varpi</math> and <math>L = \pi/M=G\pi=\varpi</math>.</ref>

<math display="block"> C = \int_0^\pi \sqrt{1+\cos^2(x)}\,dx </math>

==Other limits==

Analogously to
<math display="block">2\pi=\lim_{n\to\infty}\left|\frac{(2n)!}{\mathrm{B}_{2n}}\right|^{\frac{1}{2n}}</math>
where <math>\mathrm{B}_n</math> are [[Bernoulli number]]s, we have
<math display="block">2\varpi=\lim_{n\to\infty}\left(\frac{(4n)!}{\mathrm{H}_{4n}}\right)^{\frac{1}{4n}}</math>
where <math>\mathrm{H}_n</math> are [[Lemniscate elliptic functions#Hurwitz numbers|Hurwitz numbers]].
